title: Bounce it up and down. Does it start to swing? 2 bounces a swing: yes, 11.4 deg. 1.5: no, 0.14 deg
description:
Bounce it up and down. Does it start to swing? A bob hangs on a spring that its own weight stretches to 1 m. It is pulled 10 cm below that point with a 0.1 degree tilt from vertical and released at rest, so it bounces 10 cm up and down. Two panels share every input; only the spring differs. The left spring is tuned so the bob bounces twice per swing (k/m = 4 g/l = 39.23 s^-2, natural length 0.75 m). The right spring is tuned to 1.5 bounces per swing (k/m = 2.25 g/l = 22.07 s^-2, natural length 0.556 m). Full two-degree-of-freedom spring pendulum equations in polar coordinates, no small-angle approximation, no damping, RK4 at 1200 steps per second (0.83 ms) with a half-step check at 2400. Played in real time; deterministic, no seed.

Measured:
- swing period 2.006 s (2 pi sqrt(l/g); 2.006 s from the zero crossings of the angle between 10 and 20 s), bounce period 1.003 s on the left and 1.338 s on the right (2 pi sqrt(m/k), the same from the zero crossings of the radial speed)
- left (2 bounces a swing): the swing angle first passes 1 degree at 11.59 s and 5 degrees at 18.63 s, and peaks at 11.37 degrees at 23.82 s; that is also the largest angle in 60 s
- left: at the swing peak the bob's vertical travel is down to 1.3 cm either way over one bounce period (the last full stretch before the peak was 3.09 cm); the on-screen bounce readout (half the vertical range over the last bounce period) reads 2.3 cm at the peak and bottoms at 0.85 cm at 24.83 s; by 39.98 s the swing is back to 0.84 degrees and the bounce to 9.98 cm
- right (1.5 bounces a swing): the swing never passes 1 degree in 60 s; its largest angle is 0.141 degrees; its bounce stays at 10.00 cm
- half-step check at 2400 steps per second: 5 degrees at 18.6281 s (difference 2.2e-7 s), peak 11.3727 degrees at 23.8226 s (differences 2.0e-10 degrees, 1.9e-8 s); the right panel's largest angle 0.1415 degrees on both step sizes
- energy drift over 60 s: 3.4e-12 J/kg on the left and 4.1e-13 J/kg on the right, under 2e-9 percent of the bounce energy

Why: a swinging bob pulls hardest on its spring at the bottom of each swing and least at the two ends, so one swing tugs the spring twice. When the spring bounces exactly twice per swing, every bounce lands in step with that tug and each one pushes the swing a little more; the tiny 0.1 degree tilt is enough to start it, and the pushes add up for 24 seconds. The energy that goes into the swing comes out of the bounce, which is why the bounce fades to almost nothing at the swing peak, and then the exchange runs backwards and the bounce returns. At 1.5 bounces per swing the pushes fall out of step, cancel, and the swing never grows.

Rerun sims/springswap/springswap.py with projects/springswap/manifest.json and you get these numbers exactly.
